ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
Two simple harmonic transverse waves, $P$ and $Q$, propagate along the positive and negative $x$-axis, respectively. They have the same direction of vibration, an amplitude of 5 cm, a wavelength of ${8}\mathsf{m}$, and a wave speed of $4\mathsf{m}/\mathsf{s}$. The wave profiles of $P$ and $Q$ at $t=2.5s$ are shown in the figure. At $t=0$, wave $P$ just reaches the origin, and the particle at the origin will start to vibrate downwards from its equilibrium position; wave $Q$ just reaches $x=10\mathrm{m}$, and the particle at $x=10\mathrm{m}$ will start to vibrate upwards from its equilibrium position. After a period of time, the two waves meet.

1. Determine the equilibrium positions within the range shown in the figure where the medium's vibration amplitude is maximized due to the interference of the two waves.
2. Determine the equilibrium positions within the range shown in the figure where the medium's vibration amplitude is minimized due to the interference of the two waves.
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
Maximum equilibrium positions: x=3\mathrm{m}, 7\mathrm{m}
Minimum equilibrium positions: x=1\mathrm{m}, 5\mathrm{m}, 9\mathrm{m}

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, the horizontal axis is x/m, with the displayed range approximately from 0 to 10 m; the vertical axis is y/cm, marking ±5 cm. The dashed line is labeled P. At t=2.5 s, P is y=-5 cm at x=0, approximately passes through the equilibrium position at x=2 m, is a wave crest at x=4 m, passes through the equilibrium position at x=6 m, is a wave trough at x=8 m, and passes through the equilibrium position at x=10 m. The solid line is labeled Q. At x=0 it passes through the equilibrium position and first goes upward as x increases, is a wave crest at x=2 m, passes through the equilibrium position at x=4 m, is a wave trough at x=6 m, passes through the equilibrium position at x=8 m, and is a wave crest near x=10 m. Reasoning: It is known that the amplitude A=5 cm, the wavelength λ=8 m, and the wave speed v=4 m/s, so k=2π/λ=π/4 rad/m, ω=kv=π rad/s. P propagates along the +x direction, and after reaching the origin at t=0, the particle at the origin vibrates downward from the equilibrium position, so one may take y_P=A sin(kx-ωt). Substituting t=2.5 s, ωt=5π/2, gives y_P=A sin(kx-5π/2), which matches the phase of the dashed line P in the figure. Q propagates along the -x direction, and at t=0 the particle at x=10 m vibrates upward from the equilibrium position, so one may take y_Q=A sin(kx+ωt-5π/2). Substituting t=2.5 s gives y_Q=A sin(kx), which matches the phase of the solid line Q in the figure. The superposed displacement is y=y_P+y_Q=A sin(kx-ωt)+A sin(kx+ωt-5π/2). Using the sum-to-product formula gives y=2A sin(kx-5π/4) cos(-ωt+5π/4). Therefore at a fixed equilibrium position x, the amplitude of the resultant vibration is A_resultant=2A|sin(kx-5π/4)|. When the amplitude is maximum, |sin(kx-5π/4)|=1, that is kx-5π/4=π/2+nπ. Substituting k=π/4 gives x=7+4n, and within the range 0≤x≤10 it is x=3 m, 7 m. When the amplitude is minimum, sin(kx-5π/4)=0, that is kx-5π/4=nπ. Substituting k=π/4 gives x=5+4n, and within the range 0≤x≤10 it is x=1 m, 5 m, 9 m.
